agent_notes: The text gives no number for Isaac's age, only 'old' and 'dim eyes'. I anchor on his birth with 123 years, which is Rashi's count at 27:2 (from Seder Olam: Isaac 123, Jacob 63). That gives c. 1943 BCE, which is later than Esau's marriage at 40 (c. 1967 BCE, Gen 26:34) and agrees with Jacob 63. The margin of 5 years covers the uncertainty of the count. The tier is MACRO_ERA because the age comes from the tradition and not from the text. Against the anchor chain, anchor.jacob_birth plus 63 years would give about the same date.

Targum Pseudo-Jonathan sets the scene on the night of 14 Nisan (Passover night) at 27:1 and 27:6. This is a midrashic dating that the Hebrew does not support, so I did not use it. The day, the season and the hour stay open.

27:46 is Rebekah's pretext for sending Jacob away, with Isaac's reply and sending in 28:1-5. I put it one day after the warning with a margin of five days. It could be before the warning to Jacob (the order of verses is not a chronological claim), but I follow the verse order.

Token 12 hagadol carries the odd lemma 'gal' in the packet and STEPBible glosses it '<the> old'; the word is gadol 'big, great', and with a son it means 'elder' (older of two). I glossed it 'the elder'. The five versions split between 'eldest' (KJV, Webster) and 'elder' (YLT, ASV); with two sons 'elder' is right.

Token 5 is feminine plural ('they were dim') because eyes are grammatically feminine, although the noun carries the dual ending. I kept the plural in the literal layer ('and they were dim, his eyes'). Rashi's midrash (the angels' tears at the binding) is cited only as tradition, not as the plain sense; Rashbam, Radak and Sforno read it as old age.

kimta'te'a: a rare participle (root t-'-'), 'one who mocks / makes sport / misleads'. KJV and ASV 'deceiver' is a fair sense but loses the idea of mockery or toying; Radak glosses it 'you made sport of me'. Jacob's fear is that the father will see a mockery, not just a lie. Ramban's puzzle about the voice is quoted as his, and I do not resolve it.

STEPBible lists the lemma of הַגָּדֹל as 'גַּל' and glosses 'old'; I glossed it 'the elder/greater' (גָּדוֹל, 'big, great'), which is the sense of birth order here, matching the five English versions.
Whether the goatskins were dressed so as to feel like human hair (Sforno) is inference, not text. The commentary says so.

אָנֹכִי עֵשָׂו בְּכֹרֶךָ is grammatically open: 'I [am] Esau, your firstborn' (the flat lie) or, as Rashi reads it, 'I [am the one bringing it]; Esau is your firstborn'. The five English versions all take the flat reading. I render the Hebrew without a copula in the literal layer so the ambiguity stays visible, and the dramatic layer follows the plain reading, since the narrative (v. 24 'Are you my son Esau?') treats it as a claim of identity.

הִקְרָה (from קרה, 'to meet, to cause to happen') is rendered 'made [it] meet before me'. KJV 'brought it to me' and ASV 'sent me good speed' differ; the verb is the one behind 'chance' (miqreh), and the text has no object, so I supply [it] in brackets. Rashi's reading (Gen 27:21) that Isaac hears the unusual piety in the divine name is cited from the packet.
Rashbam's point that the twins' voices were alike, against Rashi's that Jacob's polite speech gave him away, is a real split in the commentators; I cite both without choosing.

The packet marks the final word as Ketiv/Qere: written with a final he (tzayidah, as Radak notes), read tzayid. I glossed the read form 'game' and mention the written form in the note. Radak's remark about a hint to five laws of slaughter is a midrash I only mention as such.

telyekha (hapax) is uncertain. The packet's commentaries split: Radak says quiver (and notes Onkelos renders 'your sword'), Rashi 'your sword', Rashbam quiver. The versions say 'quiver'. I follow the quiver reading, since it pairs with 'bow', and flag it here.

'Before YHWH' is Rebekah's addition to Isaac's words in v.4 (where he says 'that my soul may bless you before I die'). Radak and Ramban both read it as her raising the stakes for Jacob; I state the difference as a fact of the two texts and treat the motive as her rhetorical strategy per Radak. I did not add a motive to the dramatic layer beyond the text.

I translate 'tovim' as 'good' in the literal layer and 'choice' in the dramatic layer, following Radak (fat, fine) without importing 'fat' into the literal layer. Rashi's remark that the two kids are Isaac's own to give is rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah) and I cite it as Rashi's.

notes.note: Everything in 27:1-46 is covered by an event. Isaac's blessing of Jacob (27:28-29) and of Esau (27:39-40) are human blessings with a prophetic character, not divine speech, so I wrote no FULFILLS_PROPHECY link inside the chapter. Their fulfilments (Edom's revolt under Joram, 2 Kgs 8:20-22; Jacob's descendants ruling) lie in other books; a session on those chapters can write the links. Rebekah's promise 'I will send and fetch you' (27:45) is never shown fulfilled. Rebekah's earlier oracle (25:23, 'the elder shall serve the younger') would be the cause of the blessing event, but I did not link it because I cannot see that event's id in the packet. The ontologist or a later pass can add it.
